title: The LORD Comes Down against Samaria and Jerusalem
summary: Micah summons all peoples to hear as the LORD comes down from his dwelling, melting mountains beneath him, to judge Samaria and Jerusalem for their sins. Samaria will become a heap of rubble and its idols will be smashed. Micah laments barefoot and naked because the wound has reached Judah, and he mourns over a string of towns near his home, each named with a bitter pun, as the invader approaches the gate of Jerusalem.
story: Micah opens with his credentials and his times, then launches straight into judgment. He speaks to both halves of God's divided people, the northern kingdom of Israel with its capital Samaria and the southern kingdom of Judah with its capital Jerusalem. The northern kingdom's fall is near; Micah warns that the same sickness has spread south. This chapter begins the first of the book's three cycles, each moving from judgment to hope. The hope will not appear until 2:12-13. First Micah must make his hearers feel the approach of disaster, town by town, until it reaches the gate of Jerusalem.
historical:
Micah 1:1 places his ministry under Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, roughly from the 740s to about 700 BC. The oracle against Samaria (verses 6 and 7) must come before its fall to Assyria in 722 BC. The towns of verses 10 to 16 lay mostly in the Shephelah, the low hills southwest of Jerusalem, around Micah's home town of Moresheth-gath. Many scholars connect this lament with the Assyrian invasion of Judah by Sennacherib in 701 BC, when, by his own account, he captured forty-six fortified towns of Judah and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem, which his annals compare to caging a bird. Others suggest an earlier Assyrian campaign in the region, around 711 BC under Sargon II.

Lachish (verse 13), the most important fortress in the Shephelah, fell to Sennacherib. He had the siege carved in stone reliefs on the walls of his palace in Nineveh, now displayed in the British Museum, and excavations at Lachish have uncovered the siege ramp he built. Adullam (verse 15) was the cave where David hid when he fled from Saul (1 Samuel 22:1).
cultural:
Micah's picture of God's coming (verses 3 and 4) draws on the language of theophany, the dramatic appearance of God in storm, fire, and earthquake, familiar from Sinai (Exodus 19) and the Psalms (Psalm 18:7-15, 97:5). "High places" were hilltop shrines where Israelites often mixed worship of the LORD with Canaanite practices; Micah shockingly calls Jerusalem itself Judah's high place (verse 5).

Verse 7 speaks of the "wages of a prostitute". Temple treasure in Samaria had been gathered through worship Micah considers spiritual prostitution, and conquerors would carry it off to adorn their own temples, where it would again serve false worship. Micah's own mourning (verse 8) uses the customs of grief: wailing, going barefoot, stripping off outer garments, and cries compared to jackals and ostriches, animals whose howls haunted the desert at night. Isaiah went barefoot and stripped as a sign of coming captivity (Isaiah 20:2-4). Shaving the head (verse 16) was a common sign of mourning.
literary: The chapter has three parts: a courtroom summons with God as witness (verse 2), a theophany and verdict on Samaria (verses 3 to 7), and a lament (verses 8 to 16). The lament is one of the most intricate pieces of wordplay in the prophets. Verse 10 begins with an echo of David's lament for Saul, "Tell it not in Gath" (2 Samuel 1:20). Then nearly every town's name is turned into a pun on its fate: Beth-leaphrah (house of dust) rolls in the dust; Shaphir (beautiful) goes out in shameful nakedness; Zaanan (which sounds like go out) does not come out; Maroth (bitterness) waits for good; Lachish sounds like the word for horses, so it is told to harness its chariots; Moresheth sounds like betrothed, so it receives farewell gifts, like a bride leaving home; Achzib (deception) proves deceptive; Mareshah sounds like possessor, so a conqueror comes. The effect, in Hebrew, is like a funeral song in which every place name becomes an obituary.

outline.t: The LORD comes down to judge
Micah's lament: the wound reaches Jerusalem
A funeral song for the towns of the Shephelah

doctrines.note: God is both witness and judge (verse 2), and he comes down to deal with the sins of his own people first. Judgment begins not with the pagan nations but with Samaria and Jerusalem, the places that bore his name.
Samaria's carved images and the wealth gathered by false worship will be smashed and burned (verse 7). Idolatry is pictured as prostitution, a betrayal of the covenant relationship with God.
Mountains melt like wax when the holy God comes down (verse 4). His holiness is not a distant quality but a presence that the created world itself cannot withstand.

words.note: Bamah, high place. A raised worship site, usually on a hill. The word appears in verse 3 for the heights of the earth that God treads and in verse 5 for Jerusalem itself: "what is the high place of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem?" Micah's point is that the capital has become as corrupt as the rural shrines.

Etnan, wages, especially a prostitute's hire. Used three times in verse 7. Hosea uses a related picture of Israel's prosperity as a harlot's payment (Hosea 2:12, 9:1). The word turns Samaria's wealth into evidence of its unfaithfulness.

Makkah, wound or blow. "Her wound is incurable" (verse 9). The word can mean a blow struck by an enemy or a festering injury. Micah pictures sin as a wound that has spread from Samaria to Judah, and Jeremiah uses the same image of an incurable wound (Jeremiah 30:12).

christ: The link to Christ in this chapter is indirect. Micah's lament shows a prophet who does not announce judgment coldly; he weeps, goes barefoot, and mourns over the towns of his own region. Jesus did the same as he approached Jerusalem, weeping over the city that did not know the things that make for peace (Luke 19:41-44). The picture of God coming down from his holy dwelling in judgment (verse 3) also frames the Christian hope in a surprising way: in Jesus, God came down, not to melt mountains but to bear the wound that Micah calls incurable. The prophets describe sin as a wound only God can heal; Isaiah 53:5 says that by his wounds we are healed, and 1 Peter 2:24 applies that to Christ.

hard.q: Why does God come in judgment against his own people instead of their enemies?
hard.a: Micah's hearers probably expected God to come down against Assyria. Instead, the verdict falls on Samaria and Jerusalem. The Old Testament consistently teaches that privilege brings responsibility: the people who knew God's law and bore his name were judged by it (Amos 3:2). Micah does not say the nations are innocent (they are summoned as witnesses in verse 2 and judged in other passages), but he insists that God's people cannot treat their status as protection while practicing idolatry and injustice. Some readers find the severity troubling; others note that Micah weeps over the judgment he announces, and that the book repeatedly promises restoration after it. Judgment in Micah is real, but it is not God's last word.

questions: Micah calls Jerusalem, the religious capital, Judah's high place. Where might religious centers, including churches, become places of compromise rather than faithfulness?
Micah mourns over the judgment he announces. How does grief change the way we speak about sin and its consequences?
Micah names the towns near his home one by one. What would it mean to pray specifically for the places and people closest to you?
